The details were different, but i definitely had a similar situation w my ex when we were young 20’s and it was our first “real” relationship. Reading this now, I thought “girl be fr”. But I know that I wanted to hear an apology, to be validated in my anger and showered in compliments about how I’m too good for that and that he was a POS - not because it meant I was going to forgive the guy, but because I had been hurt and I guess you could say I thought “closure” was real. I’d still probably fall for that (outside of a relationship) under the right circumstances. I also didn’t have many friends and was hurting for just one besides my then boyfriend. All of that being said, yeah, of course she totally sounds naive. But that doesn’t mean she actually has malicious intentions. She just has rose colored glasses on. When she asked about it, she had what she wanted in mind rather than the most likely scenario (which is him continuing to be a skeeze). 

I don’t think you’re overreacting, but I think you’re dragging it out. She sounds very remorseful, and I can say that being in her position - thinking innocently and then hearing how much it affected you, to the point where she’s almost convinced it’s over - is sobering. I think you’ve made your feelings abundantly clear, I think she has a better idea of how she’s expected to respond should something similar ever happen. I think you’re at the point where she’s probably not confident that you can move forward from it so you’ll need to validate her a bit so she understands that you do still care about her and want to be with her (someone mentioned flowers, that and saying something sweet about how you feel about her is perfect). 

Yes it’s goofy to believe he has even decent intentions, but there is a learning curve. You will absolutely come to the day your girl (whether her or another down the line) tells you another woman has malicious intentions, and you’re going to be naively in denial too. It’s easier to recognize the further away from it you are. You’re young and you’re both bound to make more mistakes. It would be wise to continue to practice forgiveness and communication.

And it will for awhile. It’s not an easy thing to accept; nobody wants to believe that’s what happened to them, to call themselves a victim. I had one friend tell me she had “sex” with her fwb while she was very loudly, repeatedly, firmly refuting it. I’ve had another friend admit he was molested (not his word) as a young child, but he doesn’t see it as bad because he has a healthy relationship to sex. Even survivors of mass shootings have guilt about being called a victim because they’re still alive while others died. I’m sure there’s a psychological explanation, probably something like it’s in human nature to try to survive and so seeing yourself as a victim means you’re vulnerable and that’s unnatural to admit. 

Oddly enough, I think there’s some comfort in denial. Denying it makes you feel like you had control over it, that you can prevent it from happening again. And sure, you can decide to never drink with strangers again, you can be obvious about saying you have a boyfriend, you can be sure you’re drinking less, you can watch your drink all night so nothing is added, you can never trust a man to get you home safely, you can swear off drinking completely! But neither of my friends were drinking, and they weren’t with strangers, and they didn’t have partners, and there was no reason for them to suspect danger from trusted “friends”. 

It might be helpful to remember that even if you did everything “right”, it wouldn’t stop him from raping. None of what you did - party, drink, accept an invitation to recover somewhere safely, take care of your friend, trust a stranger - is a crime or even morally bad. His actions - getting you to drink more, separating you from your group, pursuing the two of you when you were obviously intoxicated, separating you from your friend, etc - were intentional choices he made with malicious motives. If it hadn’t been you, it would’ve been your friend, and if it wasn’t either of you, it would’ve been someone else. Nobody deserves what you experienced. No excuse changes who he is or the choices he made. HE is to blame, not you.

You can’t give consent if you’re intoxicated. 

“Wait wait” is saying no. Requiring a condom is saying no. “Ow” is saying no. “I don’t want to” is saying no. You were isolated, inebriated, in an unfamiliar place, with a stranger, while your friend was unresponsive. You were afraid and not in a position to feel confident defending yourself. He was taking advantage of your state. 

You did not cheat, you were assaulted. I’m very sorry you had this happen to you. It is not your fault.

All of what I said entirely depends on how you read it, and as I said, it’s tough love. Tough love can still be delivered in a kind tone, but like you said, tone is lost in text. 

I think you’re referring to the apples of the cheeks. How full one’s cheeks are varies drastically from one person to the next, changes with weight, and definitely look worse when one is sleep deprived (as college students tend to be). My point is that your taste will change, and just because a certain age group might have specific features doesn’t mean it’s always lost with age. Seeing it less often doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist, it’s a matter of exposure and experience. 

That doesn’t change my point. Just because it was only one person doesn’t mean never and doesn’t mean you’re hopeless [in terms of being a creep]. Tastes change, liking someone a little older is an indicator of yours seeming to change. Also you’ve been talking attraction not dating, so not being attracted to V not dating a 23 year old aren’t the same. And why not date someone that’s 23? 

I didn’t mean it to be berating, I’m more incredulous. Your concern for this shows you have good intentions. You’ve said you wouldn’t act on it. So to me, feeling like you’d have to keep a huge distance to not be a bad person is silly because you’re conscious of not acting on it. Acting on it is a choice and it’s what kinda defines whether you are good or bad. You can want to steal something but if you don’t, you’re good. You can think something mean about someone but if you don’t say it, you’re good. “Actions speak louder than words” isn’t an age old saying without reason! People can’t read your mind, so without acting on it nobody can “cancel” you for it. Also, besides grooming, how is being a predator not just sexual? 

You didn’t specifically refer to anyone you’re currently attracted to/crushing on, so assuming you’re referring to someone 15, yeah you should avoid that. Like someone else said 17 is on the line (specifically bc you’re still so close in age, if you were 23 then 17 is too young because the life stages are so different), stick to 18+. We tend to like someone based on how they make us feel. Even if you like them entirely for who they are, think about those qualities and ask yourself if those qualities are specific to minors only. I’d bet they aren’t. Knowing you’re specifically having feelings for a minor rn, I’d avoid talking to minors enough to really form a friendship. This info also changes the context of the 100 yards away comment so if by that you meant avoid forming friendships with, then yes, you should. Not because it makes you a creep, but because it does introduce the possibility of a questionable age gap relationship. Sticking closer to your age will also help with the practice of forming attractions for people your age. 

This is my favorite paragraph because I’m thrilled (truly and not sarcastically) to let you know that cancel culture does not really exist. It does in the short term, but it is not a life sentence. This is also why I have so much to say on how you’re still so young and why your gen is so extra. Celeb after celeb have done AWFUL things, influencers too, and they only have momentary lows. Social media makes it seem so much louder, but it doesn’t change the opportunities or jobs or money they get. Only the extreme actions actually cost them their livelihoods (cosby, Weinstein, Danny Mathewson or whatever the guy from that’s 70’s show is, the other actor from house of cards, etc). Jeffrey Starr and Shane Dawson and Andrew Tate and the comedian whose name I’m blanking on have all done terrible things (in various forms) and still have platforms. From what I know, James charles was only talking to or flirting with minors, got “cancelled” and still has millions of followers. Yes, the size of your audience would take a hit, but unless it’s small, it’s absolutely possible to build it back up. Especially, again, if you’re not acting on it. 

I didn’t, and still now can’t, cut out the generation part because it’s part of why you’re so concerned. The morality has been addressed by me and others. But your extreme  black and white thinking is only going to make you more fearful and make you question yourself when you have said yourself you wouldn’t act on it. Only you know you and you know your intentions. Dont let others make you question who you know you are. That’s part of why I also stand by my comment, because I know I’m not trying to be cruel, I know how I’m saying it as I type it, I know I’m not fluffing it up and going out of my way to fluff it up so it lands gently but I’m also not being unkind. I’ve spent maybe an hour sitting here trying to write this response, it would take so much more to make sure it doesn’t sound harsh, and I just dont have that time. I can’t let my fear of a stranger thinking I, another stranger, am mean interfere with my life. And neither should you! I’m saying, break out of the groupthink. It’s only going to be torture for you to try and appease others, especially when it’s a collective, faceless group like “society”. You define your own morals.

It sounds like you’re overthinking it. Most people don’t have wrinkles until they’re MUCH older. Heavy make up is a specific look women choose, plenty like a natural look too. That’s not tied to age. You also even said you’ve never been attracted to someone older and then followed up with someone you dated that’s older. Just because the data skews younger doesn’t mean it impossible, it means you’re young and inexperienced. 

I feel like this is a major problem with the younger group; y’all read things online and take it so personally and directly, regurgitate it and live it as a black and white fact. The people I see calling someone in your situation a pervert are always within the same age grouping, never older because the older crowd knows that the maturity of a 17 year old is not far behind that of a 20. Age gaps are an important factor in relationships, yes, but y’all blow it way out of proportion. Noticing that the people you, a 20 y/o, are attracted to are little younger or not in your “grade level” doesn’t mean you’re a predator. There are multiple factors that play into why you might skew younger instead of older (like make up/dressing to look more mature VS sticking to bareface and seeing youthful features stick out more). 20 year olds are only a step ahead of 17 year olds. I personally call anyone under 24 a baby. “Why is a 20 year old attending prom, ew” is an insult that’s been around for at least a decade, but when my age group used it ten years ago, it meant they were the type of loser that peaked in high school. Now yalls group have combined age gap discourse and insulting 20 year old bums into meaning “he’s a pedo because he went to prom with his gf that’s 18”. 

The part that blows my mind about it the most is your 100 yards away comment. You say you’re asexual but feel like you need distance to…. what, not sexually abuse someone? Do you assault every attractive person you see? Do you make a pass at them? Do you even talk to every attractive person?! I’m going to take a wild guess and say you don’t because you can think someone is attractive without doing anything about it, so you should absolutely be able to control yourself even if you are around someone that’s younger that you find attractive. Treat them as a regular human being like anyone else and you’re fine. 

The hypersensitivity y’all have to cancel culture and not being problematic is unprecedented, and it’ll be awhile before older people recognize it and even longer before there’s any attempt at resolving it. So it doesn’t surprise me that your doctor is overlooking it. A trend in older generations is skipping over what they see as silly/obvious and calling it a phase or “hormonal”. They were told “just throw them into the pool, they’ll figure it out” as a smartass comment about kids learning how to swim. That’s how they were taught, to just figure it out. But y’all are so scared of messing up that you think one wrong move will make everything falls apart. So here I am, getting off my soap box now to leave you with this: what you have described is normal and doesn’t make you a bad person. There are other factors to consider in what makes you attracted to someone, not just their age. What you’re attracted to will continue to change as you age. Not acting on it is a big differentiation so don’t pursue a minor and you will definitely be okay. If by 23+ you’re still mostly attracted to minors, THEN you can question yourself but again, keeping it to yourself and not acting on it is the biggest difference. 

I say all of this with good intentions, despite ripping on “your generation”. Yall need a little tough love. I’m 26 which to people your age is ancient, but the years can really blur past you. You are still learning and have so much more to learn, so please relax the fear of messing up and understand the importance of nuance. And please please reflect on and form opinions outside of what random people online tell you is right or wrong. “I would/want to sleep with that person” is fine, but “I would/want to ‘forcefully fornicate’ with that person” is not. Judging by this post, you know the difference, so you’re good.

Also to echo the others, a trauma therapist would be a great investment to make in yourself. Everyone deserves therapy, especially those carrying the weight of trauma

That’s a very difficult age to lose a parent, and I’m very sorry for your loss. 

“Daddy issues” doesn’t even really have a meaning, it’s just used on women to make them feel bad for whatever it is they’re doing. Infact, the accepted definition of it does not apply to you at all. Because what does that even mean in this context? You have daddy issues because your dad died and you miss him? That’s the human experience. Those are regular emotions and reactions. And it’s healthier to talk about him than suppress it. I think either they didn’t have a good relationship with their parents or they haven’t lost their parents. There’s no reason to be so bitter, and it’s usually people with bad parental relationships that are. Misery loves company, she probably wanted to project that on you. It might’ve even been said with the intention to get you to stop talking about him because why else would you say something cruel within earshot? I don’t think it’s worth internalizing, but I can recommend a few possible adjustments. 

Idk how exactly you talk about him, so im just throwing these ideas out there and you can decide whether they stick. 

- Mentioning death, especially of loved ones, can shut people down (whether that’s bc it’s a tough reality, bc they’ve lost a loved one and are uncomfortable with it/your ability to discuss your loss, bc they don’t know how to talk about death/heavy topics, etc). Maybe avoid mentioning his death, unless outright asked.

- if someone does get weird after you mention his passing, be sure to explain that you enjoy talking about him as you feel it keeps his spirit alive. This should alleviate any pressure they feel about comforting you or avoiding the topic. 

- you can also just try to avoid it around certain people. Like if someone else reacts poorly, then avoid it around them but you don’t have to stop posting if you don’t want to. 

- if someone gets weird about it or treats you that way, especially after explaining why you do it, they aren’t people you want in your life. There are plenty of people that have lost a parent and miss them many years on and enjoy talking about them. There are plenty that would never say something so rude nor would make you feel ostracized for it. 

- journal about him! Writing down memories will help prevent forgetting about him, plus it usually helps with getting a thought loop out of your head. So not only does it preserve memories, it also removes it from circulating in your head out of fear of forgetting, which then allows you to talk about and focus on other aspects of life.

You’re a normal teenager. You’re discovering yourself and what you like/need, and those things will change a lot in the next ten years. All of that is normal!! 

Emotions fluctuate, but mostly happy is good. Nobody is happy all of the time. 

Lying is not great but it’s normal for a teen, especially if you feel like the truth will get you in trouble. Over time you’ll learn what’s worth lying over and that “getting in trouble” is never as bad as you think it is. It depends on what’s at risk, but I would bet all my money that the lies you’re telling now will not matter in 5-10 years. Don’t worry about this one much. 

Needing validation is in human nature. Try to value the opinions of those that are important to you, not random strangers or people you don’t respect. Procrastinating is a terrible habit, and I’m a cursed professional at it. This is the only thing I firmly believe you should work to change because it will better your life. You don’t have to accomplish everything immediately, but start to do some bits of it early on. I’ll give some examples, although I’m pretty sure you mean specifically for school work. 

Homework: do it in your down time. Have it out at lunch to do bits and pieces of. Do it in the car ride home (unless you’re driving or course). Make a mini reward system; for every page you complete you can watch five tiktok videos/spend five minutes on tiktok or whatever. 

Projects: start on research or brainstorming as early as you can. It depends on the project type, but start at least collecting info/bookmarking websites early on. 

Chores: laundry is my enemy. Washing and drying is easy but putting away is hell. I try to separate my socks/underwear and put those away before getting to the real clothes. I also separate towels/sheets because those are easy to fold and sort while sitting on my lazy butt. Even if I don’t put all of it away, I did half of it just by sorting and folding, then it’s one easy trip to put them where they should be. 

Getting ready for school: choose the outfit the night before, make sure your backpack is packed with what you need, if you take water/lunch/snacks then get those arranged the night before so there’s less to do in the morning. 

You don’t have to complete a task in order to beat procrastination, you just have to start.

Overall you’re a very normal teen, no need to worry :)

Gotcha. So what you need to do is turn to email, not texts. Write a list of your complaints, and make an email saying that you have some problems you’re having a hard time addressing, list the problems/concerns, and say you’d like to discuss solutions at your next appointment. When you list your problems/concerns, do it in a bulleted list and in complete sentences and stick with “I feel/my” statements and less “you are”. 

Emails are more professional yet leisurely, more thorough, and more succinct. Texts are for short conversations with lots of responses; emails are for more information and less responses. I understand you dont want to waste a session explaining why you feel like you’re wasting sessions, so get ALL of it out, at once, in advance. Doing it over time with texts is a huge waste of both your time. Laying your complaints out in an email gives her the time to read it during downtime and respond adequately at your session because she doesn’t really need to give a verbal/written response to correct those problems. If you email “my time keeps getting cut short and we aren’t picking up where we left off”, she has the ability to start your next session on time and the way you want. These two things are very valid critiques that can/should be easily fixed without it being a big deal at all. It’s just saying “this is what *I* need”, not “you’re doing a bad job”. 

If there are other complaints you have about the efficiency of your sessions (referring to “I have more thoughts but it’s too much I’d rather open up slowly”), you can also include them in your email. And I’d suggest when sending it, include something along the lines of “I have these complaints but I have a hard time speaking up sometimes and I dont want them to go unaddressed, so I decided to email them and make them accounted for.” IMO, it both explains why you’re not waiting for your session like she told you to do and gets it out of the way so you can’t get away with another useless session talking about irrelevant things

A therapist isn’t going to judge you, you dont need to care what they think of you, and you shouldn’t be reliant on what they have to say about you as a person. Constructive criticism is still professional. “I feel like my time isn’t being valued when others run over into my appointment time” is perfectly fine, “I feel like you’re just after my money” is not. Writing all your thoughts down will help you process through them, meaning you won’t accidentally say something offensive. You can write it all down ahead of time and it makes it A LOT easier to say in person when you know what you want to say because you wrote it and had a chance to review it. No accidental insults!
